status: Four expectations have complete source-fit authoring tasks using the reviewed early-community repertoire, unchanged Egyptian daily-life knowledge and explicit supporting resource facts. No new claim, authored change or pupil attainment is inferred.

contributors.boundary: Complete two-case pre-1500 First Nation/early Inuit food, home, material-technology and setting knowledge retained; not a political/social/childhood inventory.
Whole ordinary ancient Egyptian food, crops, mudbrick family homes, children’s games/pets and then-now comparison retained. Do not infer that the wealthy Nebamun image depicts everyone.

actualCases: Egypt with separately labelled Dynastic and Roman-period material

actions: Complete both learned early-community case profiles and their independent knowledge checks from the reviewed card, with exact people/place/approximate period labels. Add the ordinary Egyptian case knowledge: named crops/foods, mudbrick homes, family activities and supported child games/pets; use a supported then-now similarity/difference to retain the complete existing Egyptian card. Label the New Kingdom Nebamun material around 1350 BCE separately from Roman-period Karanis objects. Do not collapse all Egyptian centuries into one household.

Describe significant ordinary-life aspects across all three: what people ate, where/how they lived and which material technologies supported meeting needs. Droulers cultivated and wild plants/fish and cooking/storage ceramics differ from Qariaraqyuk marine harvest, food caches and winter/seasonal dwellings. Egyptian Nile crops and mudbrick houses are specific learned facts, not a universal picture of every early society.

Explain an actual physical-setting relationship in each case using the checked source dossier. For Droulers, place the documented cultivated/gathered/fished foods and village materials in its stream/terrace/St Lawrence setting; preservation-friendly archaeological soil is not evidence that every farm had unusually productive soil. For Qariaraqyuk, use the source’s sheltered winter location, fast-ice/marine access and seasonal dwelling/harvest context. For Egypt, use the source-described Nile water/floodplain and neighbouring arid setting, not an unverified river-length ranking or the excluded map labels.

Include natural processes and their effects on food and continuing subsistence: seasonal conditions affect access to cultivated/wild food and marine harvest/storage; winter and warm-weather dwelling patterns are explicitly source-described. In the Egyptian example, the documented annual inundation deposited silt and supplied irrigation water; failed/insufficient floods threatened crops and food continuity. Keep ancient inundation distinct from present regulated river behaviour. A relationship explanation is required, not merely naming a river, season or animal. Avoid invented numeric yields, net population trends or universal ecological virtue.

Describe the importance of the local environment for meeting physical needs: connect a documented food source, water/material resource or seasonal shelter choice to food, housing or clothing in the actual studied cases. The source’s illustrative needs are not a demand to invent every clothing practice in every community. Compare a supported difference and acknowledge the source’s limits rather than make environment determine everybody’s identity or preferences.

Identify and describe significant material/technical developments and what they enabled. Use Droulers plant cultivation and ceramic cooking/storage vessels with documented stone/bone implements; early Inuit seasonal winter-house/storage and skin-boat/tool technologies from the bounded precontact sources; and Egyptian mudbrick building and agricultural water storage/canals described by the university museum. Explain a practical function and material/setting connection in each. Do not claim a group was the first inventor or that all exact engineering details survive; no tool construction, hunting reenactment or specialist physics criterion is added.

Probe independently after supported study, using a changed view or new attributed detail: which community/period does the fact fit, and how did its documented material/setting relationship work? An unfamiliar case’s information is supplied for transfer; no automatic mastery of its entire culture follows. Retain source differences between surviving objects, modern reconstruction and analogy-based historical models.
sourceLimits: The approved early-community card and Egyptian ordinary-life card remain unchanged. Additional task facts explain actual mandatory source relationships; they are not a new Egypt technology inventory or a demand for every illustrative invention.

The Kelsey museum geography discussion(pp 6–9) supplies ancient Nile inundation/material use; its map 76 is excluded. Its housing section distinguishes Dynastic evidence from Roman Karanis. Roman-period toys/household objects are never used as 1350 BCE archaeological evidence.

Whitridge2002 site facts and author-hosted2016 uncorrected synthesis are distinguished. Seasonal dwelling/boat descriptions are bounded precontact context, not proof every Qarihouse used everytechnology or a direct governance account.
No formal environment-effect attribution strength, compulsory pride, aesthetic judgment, pupil observations or practical dangerous task is inferred.
nearMiss: Uses only two cultures or lists a First Nation/Inuit case without actually describing it.
Names a river or season without explaining a supported food/material/sustainability relationship.
Calls preservation-rich excavation soil unusually fertile agricultural soil without evidence.
Gives a modern river regulation rule as the ancient annual flood cycle.
Presents the wealthy idealised painting, modern reconstruction or Roman-period toy as the everyday life of every 1350 BCE child.
Names an artefact without explaining its supported practical role, or invents a first-invention ranking.
